name: Lycopene
lead: Lycopene is the red carotenoid pigment in tomatoes, watermelon, pink grapefruit and red guava. In appearance circles it is used from the inside out: people eat cooked tomato products or take lycopene supplements to build a warmer, redder-toned complexion and to support the skin against UV-related damage [1][3][19][21]. It has no vitamin A activity, and it is also used as a food colour (E160d) [1][2].

Looksmax.org threads describe lycopene as part of a skin-colour routine alongside beta-carotene, astaxanthin and similar supplements, with posters aiming for a 'red undertone' tan or a healthier glow, and ketchup and tomato paste are discussed as inexpensive, highly bioavailable sources [19][20][21]. Carotenoids are, in dermatology terms, part of what gives normal skin its colour and a share of its natural UV defence [22].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 intervention trials found that tomato and lycopene supplementation was associated with reductions in erythema-related measures, MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and density; the authors concluded the products could act as endogenous sun protection [3]. The European Food Safety Authority, by contrast, concluded in 2011 that evidence for antioxidant effects in humans, including for skin, was insufficient [1].

Very high intake can cause lycopenemia, a harmless orange skin tint that fades after intake is reduced [1][22]. Lycopene is regarded as non-toxic in dietary amounts, with intolerance and interactions with blood-pressure drugs and anticoagulants noted [1].

paras: Lycopene is taken as a tomato-derived supplement or through cooked tomato products in the hope of photoprotection and a warmer complexion [3][4]. Topical formulations such as a lycopene emulgel have also been tested for skin biophysical parameters [5].

It is not an essential nutrient, and the median and 99th percentile of dietary intake have been estimated at 5.2 and 123 mg per day [1]. It is marketed in prostate and cardiovascular supplements on the basis of antioxidant activity [8][7].

Lycopene is a symmetrical tetraterpene built from eight isoprene units, with eleven conjugated double bonds that give it its deep red colour; it is an intermediate in the biosynthesis of beta-carotene and other carotenoids [1]. Tomatoes and tomato products supply more than 85 percent of lycopene intake for most people, while the aril of the gac fruit has been reported as the richest known source [1].

Wikipedia lists approximate amounts per serving: tomato paste about 75 mg per cup, tomato juice 22 mg per cup, watermelon 13 mg per wedge, raw tomato 4.6 mg per cup, ketchup 2.5 mg per tablespoon and half a pink grapefruit 2 mg [1]. A looksmax.org post gives its own per-100-gram table, noting that sun-dried tomatoes and ketchup are far richer than raw tomatoes [21].

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Appearance-oriented users take lycopene in three ways: whole foods (cooked tomato sauce, paste, ketchup), standalone lycopene capsules and blended skin-glow supplements, and topical products such as lycopene-containing soaps and creams [5][19][20][21]. Supplement and food routes are discussed for two aims. One is photoprotection, meaning less sunburn redness and less UV-related ageing. The other is colour, meaning a warmer or more golden-red undertone that proponents say looks healthier [3][19][20].

Because lycopene is fat-soluble, users and researchers note that cooking and eating it with oil increases absorption; thermal processing was shown in a 2002 study to raise bioaccessible lycopene in tomatoes [1][13][23]. Tomato paste can be up to four times more bioavailable than fresh tomatoes according to Wikipedia [1].

Lycopene is a highly lipophilic carotenoid, and a 1989 study reported it had the highest rate constant for quenching singlet oxygen among the carotenoids tested, higher than beta-carotene [24]. Proponents point to this antioxidant action as the reason it might blunt UV-driven oxidative stress in skin; reviews of carotenoids and sunlight discuss this possibility [4][7].

Carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layers, contribute to normal skin colour and are described as providing part of the skin's natural UV protection [22]. Lycopene is absorbed with bile salts and fat micelles, and in human blood cis-isomers make up more than 60 percent of the total [1][2].

Isolation procedures for lycopene were first reported in 1910, and its structure had been determined by 1931 [1]. Interest in lycopene as a health compound grew in the 1990s: a 1995 prospective cohort study reported on carotenoids and prostate cancer risk, and a 1999 review of 72 epidemiologic studies found that 57 reported inverse associations between tomato intake or blood lycopene and cancer at a given site, 35 of them statistically significant [25][26].

Skin photoprotection became a distinct research area with reviews around 2002 and a series of small intervention trials, summarised in the 2024 meta-analysis [3][4]. EFSA's 2011 opinion and the US FDA's 2005 decision on cancer-related labelling shaped the regulatory picture [1].

Skin: the 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 intervention trials in healthy subjects reported that tomato and lycopene supplementation was associated with significant reductions in delta-a* (redness), MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and skin density; the authors concluded it could reduce erythema and improve skin appearance [3]. A 2002 review discussed carotenoids and protection against solar UV radiation [4]. A topical lycopene emulgel trial reported improved biophysical skin parameters [5], and a registered study evaluated a tomato-extract product on skin attributes in 50 healthy participants [6].

The meta-analysis searched five databases up to January 2021, screened 19,336 publications and included 21 trials in healthy subjects; it reported significant reductions in redness (delta-a*), MMP-1, ICAM-1 and skin pigmentation, and increases in minimal erythema dose, skin thickness and skin density [3]. Many of the included trials were small, and some used industry-supplied extracts, which the wiki notes as study design context.

A completed registered study evaluated a tomato-extract product on skin attributes in 50 healthy participants, and a 2022 trial of a topical lycopene emulgel reported better biophysical skin parameters [5][6]. A 2002 review discussed carotenoids and protection against solar UV [4].

Cardiovascular and other outcomes: reviews describe an inconsistent evidence base. A 2020 review of randomized trials found conflicting evidence on cardiovascular risk factors, while a 2017 review concluded that tomato products and lycopene reduced blood lipids and blood pressure [1]. Review articles note epidemiological associations with lower cardiovascular risk with some controversy [8][7]. A registered trial tested different doses on blood pressure in pre-hypertensive adults and was terminated [9]. For prostate cancer, a 2015 review found dietary lycopene associated with reduced risk while a 2021 meta-analysis found no effect [1]; registered trials include metastatic prostate cancer [10].

Bioavailability studies show absorption is enhanced by fat and cooking and has been studied with added black pepper and oil [1][13][12]. A registered study examined lycopene and sperm quality [11]. Many skin trials are small and some use industry-supplied extracts.

Lycopene is non-toxic and commonly eaten. Reported problems include intolerance or allergic reaction with diarrhoea, nausea, stomach pain and loss of appetite, a possible increased bleeding risk with anticoagulants, and possible interactions with blood-pressure drugs. Lycopenemia, an orange skin discolouration, occurs with high intakes [1].

A 61-year-old woman who drank about 2 litres of tomato juice daily for years developed lycopenemia that faded after three weeks without tomato juice [1]. Carotenoderma from any carotenoid is described as most visible on light skin and in the palms, soles and nasolabial folds, and it spares the whites of the eyes, unlike jaundice [22].

Lycopene is a highly lipophilic antioxidant with eleven conjugated double bonds, and absorption requires bile salts and fat micelles; absorption is enhanced by fat and by cooking, and oil-based supplements may be absorbed more efficiently than food [1][2]. In human blood, cis-isomers make up more than 60 percent of total lycopene [1].

It is a symmetrical tetraterpene derived from eight isoprene units, with all-trans form predominating in plants. Isolation procedures were first reported in 1910 and the structure was determined by 1931 [1]. It is an intermediate in biosynthesis of beta-carotene and other carotenoids [1].

EFSA concluded there was insufficient evidence for antioxidant effects of lycopene in humans, including in skin and for protecting vision from UV light. In 2005 the US FDA rejected requests to allow qualified labelling for lycopene and reduced cancer risks, concluding there was no credible evidence supporting such a relationship [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: On looksmax.org, lycopene appears in threads on getting a warmer skin tone without peptides, with posters recommending lycopene and astaxanthin or all-in-one skin-glow products [19]. One poster describes combining glutathione, lycopene and kojic acid soap, aiming for a red undertone, and writes of wanting 'mogger red undertone tan skin' [20].

A looksmax.org post titled as a ketchup-as-lycopene-source guide argues that lycopene taken over a long period can change skin 'for the better' and that ketchup is cheap and highly bioavailable; a reply in that thread says the poster stopped beta-carotene after taking isotretinoin and felt unwell [21].
On T Nation the discussion focuses on prostate and urinary health, blood pressure and supplement stacks rather than skin tone [14][15][16][18]. Some members mention ketchup as a lycopene source [17].

Related inside-out skin-colour approaches discussed with lycopene include beta-carotene and astaxanthin supplements, glutathione, and carotenoid-rich diets, while topical options include self-tanners and sunscreens [19][20]. Carotenoderma, the orange skin colour produced by large carotenoid intakes, is described as benign and reversible, usually appearing after weeks of high intake and fading after months [22].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org lycopene appears in skin-tone threads, while on T Nation it appears mainly as a prostate-support or heart-health ingredient [14][15][16][19][21].

claims.claim: Lycopene (with beta-carotene) gives a warmer 'tan' and red undertone
claims.believers: Looksmax.org posters pair lycopene with carotenoids and glutathione to pursue a red-toned tan and healthier glow [19][20].
claims.experts: Carotenoids contribute to skin colour and carotenoderma shows high intake can tint skin orange, but trials of lycopene specifically have measured redness, pigmentation and thickness rather than a cosmetic tan [3][22].

claims.claim: Ketchup and tomato paste are the best lycopene sources
claims.believers: A looksmax.org post argues raw tomatoes are a poor source and ketchup is cheap with high bioavailability [21].
claims.experts: Thermal processing raises bioaccessible lycopene, and Wikipedia says tomato paste can be up to four times more bioavailable than fresh tomato [1][23].

claims.claim: Too many carotenoids can turn skin orange
claims.believers: Posters discussing beta-carotene and lycopene stacks note stopping when they felt unwell or worried about tone [21].
claims.experts: Lycopenemia and carotenoderma are documented as benign and reversible after intake is reduced [1][22].

claims.believers: Posters describe lycopene and pomegranate compounds as among the best things for the prostate and one reports less nighttime urination with a blend [14][15].
claims.experts: A 2015 review linked dietary lycopene with lower prostate cancer risk but a 2021 meta-analysis did not; regulators found no credible evidence for cancer risk claims [1].

claims.believers: A poster in his fifties reports keeping low blood pressure after adding a low-dose lycopene supplement alongside other measures [16].
claims.experts: A 2017 review concluded tomato products reduced blood pressure while a 2020 review found conflicting evidence; a registered trial was terminated [1][9].

claims.claim: Lycopene protects skin from sun damage
claims.believers: The authors of a 2024 trial meta-analysis suggest lycopene-rich products could serve as endogenous sun protection [3].
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis found improvements in erythema-related measures, though EFSA found insufficient evidence for skin antioxidant effects [3][1].

angle.text: People eat cooked tomato products or take lycopene supplements, often alongside beta-carotene, to give skin a warmer, redder undertone and to support it against UV damage. Skin trials report reduced sunburn redness measures, while forum members mainly discuss it as a tan or glow booster.
